appraisal_events.evidence: Mme de Villeparisis ne donnait, par grâce, bonne éducation, modestie réelle, ou manque d'esprit philosophique, que cette origine purement matérielle à sa connaissance de tous les arts... On aurait dit qu'il n'y avait pas pour elle d'autres tableaux que ceux dont on a hérité; and, on Balzac, Hugo, Vigny: on voyait qu'elle n'hésitait pas à leur préférer des hommes qui, peut-être, en effet, avaient eu, à cause d'elles, l'avantage sur un Balzac, un Hugo, un Vigny, dans un salon, une académie, un conseil des ministres.
appraisal_events.explanation: After the narrator and grandmother nearly took her for the measure and model of truth in all things, the passage exposes that Mme de Villeparisis's apparent connoisseurship rests on purely material, inherited grounds and that she prefers society-approved mediocrities to genuine literary genius, undercutting her earlier authority.

status_effects.explanation: Her taste is revealed to be conventional and socially/materially conditioned rather than genuinely discerning, lowering the narrator's estimation of her.
Her severe judgments against Balzac, Hugo, and Vigny in favor of minor society figures are framed as exposing flawed critical authority, weakening her position as an arbiter of taste.

ambiguities: The narrator and grandmother initially credit Mme de Villeparisis with near-infallible judgment ('la mesure et le modèle de la vérité en toutes choses'), and this trust is only gradually undercut by the closing comparison to erudite scholars banal about modern art; the passage's irony is retrospective and layered rather than a single direct statement.
